newsitem.title: UK: Hung parliament worries to weigh on UK markets.
newsitem.headline: Hung parliament worries to weigh on UK markets.

text.p: Polls show Britain's opposition Labour party heading for clear victory in the looming election but markets are beginning to fret about alternative scenarios, such as a tiny Labour majority or even a hung parliament.

Labour has long had a strong double-digit poll lead over the ruling Conservatives but that margin is gradually being whittled away. A Gallup poll this month gave Labour a 27 point lead, down from 34.5 in February.

Under the reformist leadership of Tony Blair, Labour appears to have succeeded in banishing many of the markets' anxieties about what the party would do in office. But the prospect of political instability could be unnerving.

"As the polls tighten...more and more people will begin to appreciate that a political mess is the most likely outcome of the election," said Stephen Yorke, SBC Warburg's director of economic research.
"This would undoubtedly cause a weakening of gilts and sterling. I think that'll start at the beginning of next year," he said of British government bonds and the UK currency.
The general election must be held by May 22, 1997 and May 1 is now seen as the most likely date if the government, which has a perilously thin majority of one, survives that long.
HSBC Markets economist Jonathan Loynes said it was hard to judge how much scepticism about the polls gilts had priced in already, but he expects gilts to go through a difficult patch.

The government hopes the "feel-good" factor will come to its rescue. House prices, a key barometer of the nation's sense of well-being, have been rising steadily, economic growth and consumer spending are picking up and unemployment is falling.
However, inflation could be the fly in the ointment. Incipient signs of overheating forced Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates by a quarter-point to 6.0 percent on October 30.
The shock jump in underlying inflation to 3.3 percent last month means more pre-election rate rises are on the cards.

Nevertheless, David Carlton, a lecturer in politics at Warwick University, is among some who say the Coservatives might well emerge victorious. He believes the Conservatives will secure a 10-seat majority in the new parliament.

"But I certainly don't rule out the possibility of a hung parliament," said Carlton, who correctly predicted the Conservative victory in the last general election when all the opinion polls had pointed to a Labour triumph.
He puts rock-bottom Conservative support at 42.5 percent.

"The Tories are down to the essential miminum, their vote won't go far below 42.5 percent. So my prediction is for a result more or less the same as last time, a little bit higher perhaps, because the Liberal vote is falling."

Analysts at Goldman Sachs say a weighted average of opinion polls published in October gives Labour 51.2 percent and the Conservatives 30.0 percent of the vote, versus 52.1 and 29.3 percent respectively in September.
Assuming a uniform swing, this would imply a huge Labour majority of 225 seats in the House of Commons, the lower house.
But no-one expects a result that is anything like this.

"To win a majority of just one, Labour need to win 59 seats and a national swing of four percent from the last election in 1992," Yorke said. "That is a required swing twice as large as the one of 1992 and the largest of any party since 1945."
Tom Rayner, gilts analyst at Societe Generale, believes the polls are being misleadingly kind to the opposition party.

"We believe that a Labour landslide is unlikely in the first change of government for 17 years. Also with the economy looking more healthy and unemployment falling, a last-minute recovery in the Conservatives' fortunes cannot be ruled out," he said.
Rayner forecasts an overall Labour majority of 30 to 40 seats as the most likely outcome, an estimate which tallies with the latest Reuters monthly survey of political analysts.
Opinion polls are being viewed with more suspicion because they got it so dramatically wrong in 1992.

Analysts say the reluctance of many people to admit they intend to vote Conservative, plus the usual swing-back to the government prior to the election, mean the actual gap between the parties is probably much smaller than most surveys indicate.
Yorke estimates if the published polls show Labour at 43 percent or less and the Conservatives at 36 percent or more, the most likely result will be a hung parliament.
One thing analysts do agree on is that markets will take fright if the Labour victory proves unworkably small.
"A small majority would be taken badly by the markets as the risk would be that Labour is unable to keep as firm a grip on public spending as the leadership would like," said Rayner.
He expects the gilt market to rally after the election, but says it could do so beforehand if the Labour lead remains large.
